content: The text provided appears to be a list of references from various studies and publications related to sexually transmitted infections (STIs), reproductive tract infections (RTIs), and their management, prevalence, and healthcare-seeking behaviors in different populations and settings worldwide. 1. A study conducted in public health facilities in the Gamo Gofa Zone, South Ethiopia, explored the prevalence and management of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). (J Sex Transm Dis. 2015;2015:310409). 2. Jiang et al. investigated the utilization of healthcare services by women presenting with gynecological symptoms in rural China, highlighting barriers to access and the need for improved care. (World Health Popul. 2010;11:23–37). 3. Guidelines for the management of symptomatic sexually transmitted infections emphasize evidence-based approaches to diagnosis and treatment. (Reference 134). 4. Rosenheck et al. examined treatment-seeking behaviors for STIs in high-risk populations, identifying significant gaps in care and the need for targeted interventions. (AIDS Care. 2010;22:1350–8). 5. Samanta et al. conducted a cross-sectional study in rural West Bengal, India, to assess the prevalence of reproductive tract infections (RTIs) and STI symptoms, as well as healthcare-seeking behaviors among affected individuals. (Indian J Public Health. 2011;55:38–41). 6. Hegde et al. studied RTIs among women in peri-urban underserved areas of Bangalore, India, focusing on knowledge, prevalence, and treatment-seeking behaviors. (Ann Trop Med Public Health. 2013;6:215–20). 7. Girish et al. analyzed STI morbidity patterns and treatment-seeking behaviors among female sex workers in Davangere City, Central Karnataka, India. (Int J Life Sci Biotechnol Pharma Res. 2014;3:254–60). 8. Sharma et al. conducted a community-based study to determine the prevalence of RTI symptoms and treatment-seeking behaviors among women in India. (Indian J Sex Transm Dis AIDS. 2018;39:79–83). 9. Tanton et al. reported findings from the third National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-3) in Britain, focusing on attendance and non-attendance at sexual health clinics. (Sex Transm Infect. 2018;94:268–76). 10. Tayerih et al. assessed women's sexual health knowledge and needs in behavioral clinics and shelters in Tehran, Iran, identifying critical gaps in education and services. (J Fam Reprod Health. 2019;13:26–34). 11. Jiang et al. studied HIV, syphilis, and condom use among female drug users in Maanshan, China, highlighting the intersection of substance use and sexual health risks. (Int J Gynaecol Obstet. 2010;110:158–9). 12. Ilankoon et al. explored women's knowledge and experiences of abnormal vaginal discharge in estates within the Colombo District, Sri Lanka, emphasizing the need for targeted health education. (Int J Women Health Reprod Sci. 2017;5:90–6). 13. Arrindell et al. conducted a survey on knowledge about trichomoniasis, often referred to as the forgotten STI, to raise awareness about this underdiagnosed condition. (Sex Transm Infect. 2013;89(Suppl. 1):A323). 14. Hoffman et al. demonstrated the high unmet need for STI services in remote areas of South Africa through the provision of mobile clinic services. (Sex Transm Dis. 2019;46:206–12). 15. Ekabua et al. evaluated adjuncts to case assessment for vaginal discharge syndrome in pregnant women, emphasizing the importance of accurate diagnosis. (Asian Pac J Trop Med. 2010;3:63–5). 16. Miller et al. assessed the prevalence of three STIs in a pediatric emergency department, highlighting the importance of early detection in younger populations. (Pediatr Emerg Care. 2015;31:107–12). 17. Jayapalan investigated healthcare-seeking preferences among patients with STIs attending a tertiary care center in South Kerala, India. (Indian J Sex Transm Dis. 2016;37:157–61). 18. Leichliter et al. examined confidentiality issues and the use of STI services among sexually experienced individuals aged 15–25 years in the United States. (MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep. 2017;66:237–41). 19. De Matos et al. studied the vulnerability of women engaged in sex work along prostitution and sex tourism routes in central Brazil to STIs. (Rev Lat Am Enfermagem. 2013;21:906–12). 20. Kumar explored the health-seeking behaviors of women in urban slums of Puducherry, India, regarding RTIs. (Indian J Public Health Res Develop. 2017;8:152–6). 21. Abdelrahim et al. investigated the prevalence of STIs other than HIV/AIDS among women of low socioeconomic status attending antenatal clinics in Khartoum, Sudan. (Int J STD AIDS. 2017;28:781–7). 22. Subbarao and Akhilesh assessed knowledge and attitudes about STIs other than HIV among college students in India. (Indian J Sex Transm Dis. 2017;38:10–4). 23. Malek et al. studied delays in seeking care for STIs among young men and women attending a public STD clinic. (Open AIDS J. 2013;7:7–13). 24. Denison et al. examined healthcare-seeking behaviors of individuals with STI symptoms attending a sexual health clinic in New Zealand. (NZ Med J. 2018;131:40–9). 25. Cheluget et al. analyzed changing patterns in STI syndromes in Kenya following the introduction of a syndromic management program. (Sex Transm Dis. 2004;31:522–5). 26. Grosskurth et al. evaluated the operational performance of an STD control program in Mwanza Region, Tanzania. (Sex Transm Infect. 2000;76:426–36). 27. Garcia et al. demonstrated improved STI syndrome management through a network of clinicians and pharmacy workers in Peru. (PLoS ONE. 2012;7:e47750). 28. Khan et al. developed and assessed a syndromic case management approach for STIs in public sector facilities in Punjab, Pakistan. (Ann Glob Health. 2014;80:486–92). 29. Kisa and Taskin validated the symptomatic approach used by nurses in diagnosing vaginal infections. (J Clin Nurs. 2009;18:1059–68). 30. Mahmood and Saniotis evaluated the use of a syndromic management algorithm for STIs and RTIs in community settings in Karachi, Pakistan. (J Pak Med Assoc. 2011;61:453–7). 31. Banneheke et al. assessed the validity and reliability of the WHO syndromic algorithm for vaginal discharge as a screening tool for trichomoniasis. (Ann Trop Med Public Health. 2016;9:43–7). 32. Barry et al. evaluated the accuracy of syndromic management in targeting vaginal and cervical infections among symptomatic women in Dakar, Senegal. (Trop Med Int Health. 2018;23:541–8). 33. Das et al. assessed the prevalence and clinical management of STIs among female sex workers in two cities in India. (Infect Dis Obstet Gynecol. 2011;2011:494769). 34. Desai et al. studied the prevalence of STIs and the performance of STI syndromes against etiological diagnoses among female sex workers in Surat, India. (Sex Transm Infect. 2003;79:111–5). 35. Francis et al. highlighted the inadequacy of syndromic management for curable STIs among women at increased risk for HIV in northwestern Tanzania. (PLoS ONE. 2014;9:e101221). 36. Garcia et al. investigated RTIs among rural women in the highlands, jungle, and coastal regions of Peru. (Bull World Health Organ. 2004;82:483–92). 37. Lima et al. compared syndromic and clinical nursing approaches for managing vaginal discharge in pregnant women in Brazil. (Rev Esc Enferm USP. 2013;47:1265–71). 38. Moherdaui et al. validated STI flowcharts for syndromic management of vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain in Honduras. (Rev Med Hondur. 2005;6:263). 39. Molaei et al. conducted a comparative evaluation of diagnostic methods for bacterial vaginosis. (Kuwait Med J. 2018;50:205–12). 40. Msuya et al. assessed the effectiveness of a syndromic approach in managing vaginal infections among pregnant women in northern Tanzania. (East Afr J Public Health. 2009;6:263–7). 41. Onyekonwu et al. evaluated etiological agents and syndromic management of vaginal discharge in Lagos, Nigeria. (Niger J Med. 2011;20:155–62). 42. Romoren et al. highlighted the inadequacy of syndromic management for trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis during pregnancy in Botswana. (Bull World Health Organ. 2007;85:297–304). 43. Tann et al. reported the lack of effectiveness of syndromic management in targeting vaginal infections during pregnancy in Entebbe, Uganda. (Sex Transm Infect. 2006;82:285–9). 44. Vallely et al. evaluated the performance of syndromic management for detecting and treating genital infections among women in Papua New Guinea. (BMJ Open. 2017;7:e018630).
